title: The Ensoniq ES5506 OTTO registers
covers: the sixteen register addresses of the Ensoniq ES5506 OTTO sound device, whose meaning the page register selects, as its specification describes them and as MAME's device handles them

rows.text: The global registers, the page register among them, can be reached at all times, whichever voice page is selected.
The registers follow the Motorola 68000 address conventions: the page register and its lowest byte are at different locations of the chip's space.
The page register selects one of the sixty-five pages through which a voice's registers are addressed.
A write to the page register stores the page the following accesses address.
MAME stores the page in seven bits and does not refuse the pages above 0x40, where the document says sixty-five pages are accessible.
A read of the page register returns the stored page number, in all three page blocks.
The voice interrupt vector holds the number of the voice that caused an interrupt, so the processor can find it.
Bit 7 monitors the IRQB output line and bits 4 through 0 hold the voice number.
A read returns the voice number, and the IRQB output line goes high after the processor reads the register.
MAME returns the vector, clears it to 0x80 and drives the IRQ callback low, where the document says IRQB goes high; the test page's read only returns it.
A write to the vector register does nothing: its case holds only a break.
The vector reads 0x80 when the device starts, before any voice has interrupted.
MAME latches the voice number into the vector and clears that voice's IRQ bit only while the vector's bit 7 is set.
The register holds the ten-bit digital value of the A/D conversion for pots and wheels, compared against an internal reference of 2.8 V.
A read starts a conversion by discharging the capacitor and counting the input, then loads the counter value, leaving 0x3FF if the input never reaches the reference.
The converter suits slow analog controls scanned about 300 times a second and read at each timer request.
MAME returns the board callback's value masked to ten bits and starts no conversion; without a callback it returns zero.
A write to the pot register does nothing: its case holds only a break.
Each voice's twenty registers are spread over two pages, all of them reached through the page register.
The control register is a 16-bit register that directs the modes of a voice.
The bank select bits are output on BS[1:0] with the address of a memory cycle, choosing among four 2-megasample banks in an 8-megasample system.
CMPD selects compressed rather than linear sample data from sound memory.
CA2 to CA0 name one of six serial output channels; voices sharing a channel may need their volumes lowered against overflow.
LP4 and LP3 set the last two filter poles to low or high pass; poles one and two are always low pass with coefficient K1.
IRQ is a status flag showing that the voice requested service or waits for the interrupt vector to be cleared.
DIR gives the address direction, zero forward and one backward, and bidirectional looping toggles it at the loop ends.
IRQE enables the voice's interrupt.
LPE and BLE encode the looping states; with both zero the accumulator stops at loop end, and the start and stop roles swap when DIR is set.
LEI makes the chip ignore the loop end check, which the trans-wave mode needs so the accumulator does not stop; the mode makes loops that evolve rather than sound stagnant.
STOP1 stops the address ALU from changing the voice's accumulator or direction, so the processor can write them.
The document advises writing a register twice, at least three microseconds apart, while a voice runs, because the pipeline may overwrite it.
STOP0 has the same effect as STOP1 and is also set by the address ALU at loop end; both must be zero for the voice to run.
The loop start register is a 21-bit value with no fractional part, giving where the accumulator jumps at loop end.
A write stores the loop start position.
The frequency control register is 17 bits, six integer and eleven fractional, and sets how far the address ALU steps each sample.
A write stores the frequency count.
Page 64 addresses twelve channel registers of 23 bits, whose lower twenty bits go to the serial output and saturate on overflow.
With the page register's test bit set, the processor can write a channel register and its data is shifted out of the serial output.
Channel 0's left and right registers accumulate the voices assigned to channel 0 and feed serial port 0.
A write to channel 0's registers is shifted out of the serial port.
The channel registers are reached only for testing: they can be written, but not read.
MAME stores the control register's sixteen bits as written.
A write to channel 0's left register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 0 left test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1267 and returns.
A write to channel 0's right register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 0 right test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1271 and returns.
The end register, also called the loop end register, is 25 bits: 21 integer and 4 fractional, marking the end of a loop for finer control.
When the direction bit is set, the start and end registers exchange their roles.
A write stores the loop end position.
The accumulator is 32 bits: 21 integer bits fetch the sample and 11 fractional bits give the frequency resolution and the interpolation.
The accumulator starts as the waveform's beginning, unlike the loop start register, which marks the start of the sustain part.
The document notes that a write to the accumulator may be overwritten when the chip increments it for an active voice.
The left volume register is 16 bits: a 4-bit exponent in the most significant bits, an 8-bit mantissa below, and four low bits for fine ramp control.
When STOP1 or STOP0 is set, the left volume is ignored and the volume is set to zero.
The document notes that a write to the left volume may be overwritten while the envelope hardware increments it.
The left volume ramp register holds an 8-bit ramp amount in its most significant bits, and its eight low bits are not implemented.
A write stores the ramp amount the envelope hardware adds to the left volume.
Channel 1's left and right registers work as channel 0's and feed serial port 1.
A write to channel 1's registers is an access for testing, in the same way as channel 0's.
MAME stores the accumulator through its address-accumulator shift.
MAME stores the left volume's sixteen bits as written.
A write to channel 1's left register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 1 left test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1275 and returns.
A write to channel 1's right register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 1 right test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1279 and returns.
The right volume register sets the right channel's amplitude; its contents match the left volume's and together they pan the signal.
When STOP1 or STOP0 is set, the right volume is ignored and the volume is set to zero.
The right volume ramp register holds an 8-bit ramp amount in its high bits, and its eight low bits are not implemented.
A write stores the ramp amount the envelope hardware adds to the right volume.
The filter storage registers are temporary 18-bit storage for each voice's real time filters, addressable for testing and initialization.
The registers keep updating while the voice is stopped, and a voice should not start before the four filter temp registers clear the invalid data.
The O4(n-1) register holds the filter's final stage output, the data presented to the volume multiplication and channel accumulation.
The O3(n-1) register holds the third stage's output, which becomes the fourth stage's input and is pushed into O3(n-2) on the next cycle.
A write stores the filter value as an 18-bit value.
Channel 2's registers work as channel 0's and feed serial port 2.
A write to channel 2's registers is an access for testing, in the same way as channel 0's.
MAME stores the right volume's sixteen bits as written.
A write to channel 2's left register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 2 left test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1283 and returns.
A write to channel 2's right register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 2 right test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1287 and returns.
The envelope count register is a nine-bit counter that sets a ramp's duration, decrementing once per sample period.
When the counter reaches zero, the envelope calculation stops updating the voice's volume and filter coefficients.
While the envelope counter is zero, the filter coefficients and volumes can be changed without the pipeline overwriting them.
The document advises writing zero to the counter, then the new value one sample period later, or writing it twice; a non-zero value may be overwritten.
A write stores the counter's starting value.
The K2 register is 16 bits with the twelve most significant used, and sets the 3 dB point of the filter's third and fourth poles.
The document notes that a write to K2 may be overwritten while the hardware envelope increments the filter value.
A write stores the filter coefficient 2.
The O3(n-2) register stores the third stage's output from the previous sample, which the high pass mode of pole 4 needs.
A write stores the filter value as an 18-bit value.
The O2(n-1) register holds the second stage's output, which becomes the third stage's input and is pushed into O2(n-2) on the next cycle.
A write stores the filter value as an 18-bit value.
Channel 3's registers work as channel 0's and feed serial port 3.
A write to channel 3's registers is an access for testing, in the same way as channel 0's.
A write to channel 3's left register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 3 left test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1291 and returns.
A write to channel 3's right register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 3 right test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1295 and returns.
The K2 ramp register holds an 8-bit ramp amount in its high bits; its least significant bit, when set, adds the increment every eight sample periods.
A write stores the ramp amount and the slow-mode control bit.
The K1 register is 16 bits with the twelve most significant used, and sets the 3 dB point of the filter's first, second and third poles.
The document notes that a write to K1 may be overwritten while the hardware envelope increments the filter value.
A write stores the filter coefficient 1.
The O2(n-2) register stores the second stage's output from the previous sample, which the high pass mode of pole 3 needs.
A write stores the filter value as an 18-bit value.
The O1(n-1) register holds the first stage's output, which becomes the second stage's input.
A write stores the filter value as an 18-bit value.
Channel 4's registers work as channel 0's and feed serial port 4.
A write to channel 4's registers is an access for testing, in the same way as channel 0's.
A write to channel 4's left register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 4 left test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1299 and returns.
A write to channel 4's right register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 4 right test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1303 and returns.
The active voice register holds how many voices are enabled, in its five low bits, values 31 to 0; the number active is one more than the value.
The number of active voices sets the output sample rate: at 16 MHz, 32 voices give a 31.2 kHz rate, and at 16.9 MHz 24 voices give 44.1 kHz.
The register initializes to 32 when RESB is asserted, and at least five voices must be enabled.
The sample rate is a formula of the master clock, sixteen and the number of voices; the scan's operator between them is doubtful.
A write stores the number of active voices, from which the chip derives its sample rate.
The word clock start register holds a 7-bit value: the number of bit clocks after an LRCLK transition before the word clock is asserted.
A write stores the word clock start value.
The word clock end register holds a 7-bit value: the number of counts after an LRCLK transition before the word clock is negated.
A write stores the word clock end value.
The K1 ramp register holds an 8-bit ramp amount in its high bits; its least significant bit, when set, adds the increment every eight sample periods.
A write stores the K1 ramp amount and its slow-mode control bit.
Channel 5's registers work as channel 0's and feed serial port 5.
A write to channel 5's registers is an access for testing, in the same way as channel 0's.
A write to channel 5's left register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 5 left test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1307 and returns.
A write to channel 5's right register stores nothing: the case calls LOG("Channel 5 right test write") at src/devices/sound/es5506.cpp:1311 and returns.
The mode register has five bits that control the serial data system's clocks and the dual and slave operation of the chip.
LRCLK_EN enables the LRCLK pin as an output when clear and is set high, as an input, when RESB is asserted.
WCLK_EN enables the WCLK pin as an output when clear and is set high when RESB is asserted; the chip does not use WCLK for its own timing.
BCLK_EN enables the BCLK pin as an output when clear and is set when RESB is asserted.
Mode 1 and Mode 0 encode four modes of operation for single and dual OTTO systems.
The memory master drives RASB, CASB, AMUXB and E; in a two-chip system the slave synchronizes to the master's E pin and they alternate memory cycles.
On reset the mode bits initialize to MODE1=1 and MODE0=0, a dual OTTO slave with normal addressing.
The early address mode suits a single OTTO in a ROM-only system, moving the address change half a cycle earlier.
A write stores the five mode bits.
The left/right clock end register holds a 7-bit value: the number of bit clocks the LRCLK output stays high.
A write stores the left/right clock end value.
A write to register 0x60 in the test page stores nothing: its case holds only a log and a break.
